parcalar.metin: [excited, emphatic science storyteller] How do blades longer than a hundred meters turn wind into electricity? Energy Sources, episode two: wind!
Wind is actually solar energy. The sun heats the Earth unevenly. Warm air rises, and cooler air rushes in to replace it. That flow is wind.
Blades are built from layers of glass and carbon fiber, cast in one piece with resin in giant molds. Today, some blades are over a hundred meters long.
The housing on top of the tower is called the nacelle. Inside are the main shaft, in most turbines a gearbox, and the generator. Some turbines have no gearbox at all; the generator turns directly.
The giant blades travel on special extendable trailers. Sometimes the whole route is planned just to get around the bends.
On site, a concrete foundation is poured first. Giant cranes stack the tower sections, then lift the nacelle and blades more than a hundred meters up.

[dramatic] When the wind blows, the blades create lift like an airplane wing, and the rotor turns. The generator converts that rotation into electricity, a transformer steps up the voltage, and power flows into the grid.
The turbine turns itself to face the wind. When a storm gets too strong, it changes the angle of its blades, slows the rotor and protects itself.
[excited] No fuel, no smoke; just moving air. Next episode: the power of water! Follow Kozmos Lab.
